text: School age is a bureaucratic threshold, and a father who has kept his daughter fed in a shack the state does not recognize learns what crossing it costs. Leon Dai gives the situation ninety-two minutes and refuses to enlarge any part of it: the poverty is not styled, the officials are doing their jobs, the girl is a child rather than a lesson. Taiwan submitted the film to the Academy, the Golden Horse jury named it best feature, and it joined that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films - an odd career for a picture whose central drama is a father trying to prove that he is one. What stands to be lost is not the house. It is the ordinary permission to remain a family, which turns out to rest on documents nobody thought to keep.

The bargain arrives early: a daughter may have her education so long as everyone she meets believes she is a son. Li Han-Hsiang places that arrangement in the fourth century and films it in Hong Kong in 1963 as a musical, which alters the temperature completely - a premise that could be wound for suspense is instead tuned for melody. Two hours of studio-made antiquity. The running time does not go on plot; a musical would rather repeat a feeling than advance one, and repetition is what a disguise does to a person's days. The Golden Horse jury named it best feature, and it holds a place on that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films. Concealment is treated here as a condition of learning, and the singing carries what the speaking is not allowed to.

Two stories run side by side here, and both turn on what a life costs when it can be bought. Jou is trying to begin again with a man named Che; Wei is saving toward the freedom of a dying young woman named Fumiko. Wang Tung takes 175 minutes over 1920s Taiwan, a length that lets the place hold work and weather rather than serve as a backdrop for grief. The structure is not decorative. Setting a courtship beside a purchase forces each to be read through the other, so tenderness keeps acquiring a price and the price keeps acquiring tenderness. The Golden Horse jury named it best feature, and it sits on that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films. What accumulates across three hours is not suspense but arithmetic: every affection in it has already been quietly costed.

An American bomb lands in a village field and does not go off, which for these farmers is less a catastrophe than a question of what it might be worth. Wang Tung sets the film in the last months of Japanese rule over Taiwan and keeps the war at the edge of the frame, audible and useless; what occupies the village is rice, family, and the daily accounting of too little. The comedy lives in that gap. People with nothing look at a weapon and see metal, or luck, and the film lets the joke stand without softening the hunger underneath it. Ninety-six minutes, no lecture. It took the Golden Horse for best feature and later joined that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films, though what stays is the tone: funny while the ground keeps giving way.

Three generations have each produced one son, and the last of them sits in a cell waiting to be executed for theft. Lee Hsing builds the film around the grandmother who will not accept that arithmetic, which turns a legal matter into a family negotiation and the negotiation into something harder: what a family is owed by the law, and what a condemned man owes anyone. Ninety-nine minutes, and the crime is settled before they start. Taiwan sent it to the Academy, the Golden Horse jury named it best feature, and it holds a place on that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films. The premise sounds like a moral test with an obvious answer. It is arranged so that mercy and justice keep charging each other, and the film declines to make the arrangement comfortable.

A state agricultural council supplies the inciting incident: a flock of genetically improved ducks, handed to a widowed farmer and his daughter for a breeding trial. Lee Hsing does not disguise that origin. The modernization of a countryside is the film's open business, and the household story grows inside the policy rather than beside it, which is rarer than it sounds. What the 110 minutes actually hold is small - feed, water, weather, animals kept alive by hand, and a girl growing up inside that labor. The Golden Horse jury named it best feature, and it appears on that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films. Watched now it works partly as a document: of a decade, of an agency, and of a moment when a film could look for its drama in livestock.

The source is a real life: Zheng Fengxi, disabled from childhood, who studied his way to a college degree and then wrote it down. Lee Hsing gives that 110 minutes, a long span for a story whose events are mostly effort - no reversal to build toward, no antagonist beyond circumstance and other people's assumptions about what a body can do. So the interest falls on how the film handles time. Repetition is the material: the same work, attempted again, and then again, until accumulation itself becomes the event. The Golden Horse jury named it best feature and it appears on that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films. What the film asks of a viewer is patience with persistence, and a willingness to find persistence dramatic.

Part One ends without ending, because it was built as half of something and knows more is coming. Evan Yang follows one man, Xu, and the three women whose lives cross his while the Second World War works away in the background - not as spectacle, but as the force that keeps rearranging where people happen to be standing. The arrangement is symmetrical by design: one man, three women, one war. Ninety-nine minutes is short for that, and the compression shows; feeling arrives fast and is interrupted faster. The Golden Horse jury named it best feature and it sits on that award's hundred greatest Chinese-language films. Melodrama built on a war runs on a particular contract, in which everything the characters want stays subject to something none of them can touch.

The carry-on is the argument: everything Ryan Bingham owns fits inside one, and he regards that as an accomplishment rather than a symptom. A man paid to walk into offices and tell strangers their jobs are gone, he has built a life from which nothing can be taken. Jason Reitman released that premise in 2009, which gave the firing scenes a temperature no screenplay could have engineered alone. The National Board of Review named it the year's best film; the Writers Guild honored the adaptation. What complicates the comedy is a woman who travels as he does, and a milestone he has spent years counting toward - ten million miles, the reward for which turns out to be a number. The arithmetic is played straight, and the jokes are never allowed to cover the transaction underneath them.

A revenge western set in 1825 Tasmania, where the chase leads not across open country but into wilderness that closes behind everyone who enters it. Clare is Irish, twenty-one, and a convict, which in this colony means her word weighs nothing against a British officer's; the only route left runs on foot, at the pace of two people with no reason to trust each other. Jennifer Kent pairs her with an Aboriginal tracker carrying his own history of what the same colony has done, and refuses to let either stand in for the other. 136 minutes is a long walk. The length is the method: violence costs something in duration as well as in image, so none of it passes as style. The AACTA named it the year's best film and honored three of the performances.

Ballet remakes a body in small increments, and the teenager at the center of this film is submitting to that discipline while also trying to make the same body hers. Lukas Dhont keeps the drama inside the training rather than around it, which is the governing decision - the school is not a setting but the mechanism, its mirrors and daily measurement doing work that a weaker version would hand to speeches. 105 minutes, one point of view, very little relief. The pressure is physical and it is scheduled: a timetable the body must meet, set against a timeline the body will not keep. The Caméra d'Or went to it, and European audiences voted it their film of the year at the European Film Awards.

The bridge has no military value; the film establishes that early, and keeps the boys on it anyway. Bernhard Wicki staged this in 1959, in the country that had lived it, from a West German novel written against the war by Gregor Dorfmeister. The horror is in the direction of traffic: beaten Wehrmacht soldiers streaming away from the Americans, schoolboys arriving with their blood-and-honor slogans intact, each side certain it understands the moment. Wicki takes the boys' conviction seriously enough to show where it was issued from, which is harder than mockery. Most of the 103 minutes go to who these children were before the order came, so the order lands on people rather than on a position. The German Film Awards gave it best feature and best direction.

Boredom is the engine: a handful of young people in front of a Munich apartment building, with nothing to do and no plans to find anything. Rainer Werner Fassbinder gets ninety minutes out of that stasis, which is a dare - idleness has to stay legible without a plot arriving to relieve it. Then Jorgos moves in from Greece, and the group discovers it has opinions. What follows works less as a story than as a demonstration: how quickly emptiness organizes itself around a stranger, how the talk hardens, who repeats what, who profits by it. The German Film Awards recognized it as a best feature and it appears on Die wichtigsten deutschen Filme. The cruelty stays casual throughout, traded between people who would never use that word about themselves.

Hamburg, 1944: there is a war on, and there is also a murderer, and it is the murderer the police cannot manage. Robert Siodmak films the hunt as procedure - legwork, files, a case assembled by men doing a job - and then lets that case collide with the state that employs them, since an uncaught killer in 1944 is not only a crime but an embarrassment with political consequences. That collision is what the film runs on: the investigation is hazardous to conduct. West Germany made it in 1957, twelve years after the events it stages, and the proximity shows in how little the period needs explaining. 100 minutes, tight. It was sent as an international submission to the Academy Awards and stands on Die wichtigsten deutschen Filme, with a German Film Award for best feature.
